The One Nobody Saw Coming

The Griffith had the muscle. The Chimaera had the manners. The Tuscan had the theatrics. The Tamora arrived with something none of them quite possessed: the ability to make TVR’s extraordinary performance feel remarkably natural. And almost nobody noticed.

By Oliver Bacon · 16 minute read

350 bhp
From a 3.6-liter straight-six TVR built itself
333 bhp
For every 1,000 kg (2,205 lb). More than a Ferrari 360 Modena
356
Delivered, 2002 to 2006. The Chimaera sold more than 5,000
4.4 sec
0–60 mph, in the TVR built for after the office

There is a peculiar sort of tragedy in being the sensible member of an unreasonable family. Imagine growing up with siblings who can’t do anything quietly: a muscular troublemaker with an appetite for confrontation, an elegant gentleman with a fondness for long weekends and expensive hotels, a flamboyant exhibitionist determined to attract every pair of eyes within 100 yards and, youngest of all, an uncompromising psychopath with the looks of a road-going race car.

And then there is you: athletic, capable, reasonably well-mannered and perhaps a little awkward-looking, with most of the family’s talents and none of its desperate need to announce them. You are quicker than people expect and perfectly happy to let your siblings have the spotlight. Welcome to the life of the TVR Tamora.

It was supposed to be the approachable one, the TVR you could drive home after a long day at work, take away for a weekend and enjoy on a quiet Sunday morning without feeling that it was plotting your demise. The remarkable thing is that TVR largely succeeded. The unfortunate thing is that hardly anyone seemed to care.

Beneath that slightly unusual bodywork was a genuinely accomplished sports car, praised by the testers of the day for its steering, its balance and the way it talked to the driver. It was still ridiculously fast, temperamental, loud and thoroughly British. But for perhaps the first time, TVR had built a car that didn’t make its driver worry quite so much about what might happen next. It wasn’t the most beautiful member of the family, nor the fastest or the most celebrated. It might, however, have been one of the best to drive.

The briefReplacing a favorite is never easy

To understand the Tamora, go back to the 1990s, when the Griffith and the Chimaera had given TVR a remarkably effective formula: light construction, plenty of V8 power and the sort of individuality bigger manufacturers could only envy. The Chimaera became TVR’s best seller, with more than 5,000 built by the most cautious count and over 6,000 by TVR’s own. It was a difficult act to follow.

By the turn of the millennium, the Rover-derived V8 behind both cars was nearing the end of its role. TVR had invested heavily in engines of its own, its Speed Six was already in the Cerbera and the Tuscan, and the muscular curves of the 1990s were giving way to shapes that looked as though they had arrived from another civilization. The question was what to do about the customer who wanted TVR performance without the most extreme version of that future. That customer was supposed to buy the Tamora.

It was previewed at the 2000 British Motor Show at Birmingham’s NEC, came back revised in 2001 and reached customers in 2002. Its name came from Tamora, Queen of the Goths in Shakespeare’s Titus Andronicus, hardly the most mild-mannered character Shakespeare ever wrote. But this was TVR, and even its sensible sports car was named after a ruthless, vengeful queen. Built on the Tuscan’s more modern chassis with TVR’s own Speed Six, and aimed squarely at the Porsche Boxster and the Mercedes-Benz SLK, it wasn’t simply a replacement. It was an attempt to redefine what an everyday TVR could be.

The faceThe face that launched a thousand arguments

We might as well address the elephant in the room. The Tamora is not conventionally beautiful. There, I’ve said it. In a family that includes the Cerbera’s exquisite profile and a Tuscan that looks like a concept car on the run, it was always going to struggle in a beauty contest. The headlights sit in large, dark recesses, the nose is short and rounded, and the whole car looks a little surprised by its own existence: muscular and purposeful from some angles, slightly startled, almost amphibian, from others.

Its proportions were driven as much by practicality as by visual theater. It shared the Tuscan’s wheelbase but cut the overhangs back hard at both ends, so at 3,925 mm (154.5 in) it was barely longer than a Griffith, easy to place in traffic and easy to park. Its body was compact because it was supposed to be useful.

Even inside TVR, the styling divided people. The body was drawn mainly by Lee Hodgetts and Darren Hobbs, with TVR designer Damian McTaggart helping, mostly on the interior, and Ralph Dodds, in TVR: Cars of the Peter Wheeler Era, records McTaggart’s verdict: “I hated the Tamora – the proportions are all wrong.” That points to a real problem. TVR buyers expected cars that were spectacular to look at, and the Tamora’s best qualities weren’t obvious from the curb. You had to drive it.

Judge it instead as a compact British roadster, and the short overhangs, broad shoulders and tight packaging look athletic rather than odd. The Tamora doesn’t look dressed for an audience. It looks dressed for the drive, and that, I suspect, is precisely the point.

The specsThe sensible TVR. Which is to say, not very sensible at all.

Consider TVR’s idea of an approachable sports car: a 3.6-liter straight-six making 350 bhp at 7,200 rpm, rear-wheel drive, a 5-speed manual, around 1,050 kg (2,315 lb), no traction control, no stability control, no anti-lock brakes and a claimed 160 mph. This was the company’s answer to the Boxster and the SLK, and somebody in Blackpool clearly had a tremendous sense of humor.

Dollars at 2001’s average exchange rate (about $1.44 to the pound); 2026 figures use UK consumer price inflation (in2013dollars) and about $1.33 to the pound. Independent test results may vary.

The original Boxster 2.5 of 1996 made 201 bhp, and the early Boxster S around 250. The Tamora had another 100 horsepower and weighed considerably less, about 333 bhp for every 1,000 kg (2,205 lb), and Dodds points out that it beat a Ferrari 360 Modena of the same era on power for its weight. It matched the supercharged SLK32 AMG for power, with the manual gearbox the AMG never offered, while weighing about 345 kg (761 lb) less. And it had nearly 3 times the power of the Lotus Elise, the car its steering would soon be compared with.

This wasn’t a watered-down TVR. It was a concentrated one, never meant to be slow or soft, only easier to enjoy.

The chassisThe athlete who knew when to relax

This is where the Tamora separates itself from its siblings. Having performance and being able to use it are not the same thing, and the best sports cars do more than respond to commands. They make the driver feel connected. TVR’s chassis engineer Ben Lang took the Tuscan’s chassis and deliberately softened it. The Tamora rode on smaller 16-inch wheels with taller-sidewall tires, its suspension was tuned to soak up bad surfaces, and its electro-hydraulic power steering gave more help in town and less as the speed rose, so the front wheels felt closer the faster you went. It didn’t just make the steering lighter. It made it better.

The press noticed. Angus Frazer, who drove the only Tamora in existence in the early summer of 2001, found a TVR that no longer called for “the fight-or-flight reactions of a toreador,” and he compared its steering with the Lotus Elise’s, then the benchmark. Richard Meaden put it more simply in evo: “Here is a TVR that can be driven hard like a Boxster.” From a magazine that knew exactly how intimidating a TVR could be, that was an extraordinary compliment.

The best proof came on a miserable night, with Dodds himself in the passenger seat of a dealer’s demonstrator. On a patch of wet leaves, the tail stepped out. He is fairly sure a Griffith or a Tuscan would have finished in the ditch facing the wrong way. The Tamora was gathered up with a single small, quick movement of the driver’s wrists, and the journey carried on as though nothing had happened.

None of this came from electronics. The driver still had to understand weight transfer, throttle and grip, but the Tamora made the consequences easier to see coming. What it offered was confidence, not the artificial kind a computer provides but the kind that comes from a chassis talking clearly to the person behind the wheel.

The driveThe pleasure of a good road

Imagine an early Sunday morning somewhere in the British countryside. The roads are quiet, the surface is still damp beneath the trees, the roof is down, and ahead lies a run of bends that tighten and open with the hills. In a more aggressive TVR, most of your attention would go into managing the power and watching the rear axle.

The Tamora invites you to settle into a rhythm instead. The steering tells you what the front tires are doing, the suspension stays composed without cutting you off from the road, and the engine builds its power progressively. You trust it, not blindly, because there isn’t a single electronic safety net, but enough to brake, turn in, feel the nose take a set and feed in the power as the road opens. One corner becomes another, and arriving starts to matter less than getting there.

There is a delicious irony in that. The sensible member of the family may have been one of the most enjoyable to drive with real commitment, not because it was less of a TVR, but because it was better at letting you enjoy being in one.

The engine6 cylinders, 1 very different personality

Under the hood was TVR’s own Speed Six, a naturally aspirated straight-six with twin overhead camshafts and 4 valves per cylinder, here in its smaller 3,605 cc form. Where the old Rover V8s handed over their performance with an almost casual surplus of torque, this one wanted to rev, with peak power arriving at 7,200 rpm. You worked the gearbox, let it climb and enjoyed the delivery growing more urgent toward the top.

The deep V8 rumble gave way to a sharper, more mechanical voice, and some owners missed the old one. Ian Dally, an owner we’ll meet again, fitted an aftermarket exhaust within the first couple of years because the straight-six simply didn’t sound as good as a TVR V8. But it suited a car that was about working with the road rather than overwhelming it, and it was never slow. TVR claimed 0–60 mph in 4.4 seconds and 100 mph in 9.5, still enough today to make a properly driven Tamora feel genuinely fast.

The cabinA TVR you could live with. Almost.

Inside, TVR ignored convention as usual: no ordinary dashboard, just sweeping forms, unusual instrument placement and adventurous trim in a cabin that looked as though it belonged to a far more exotic car. You didn’t merely sit in a TVR. You entered one.

But the Tamora also had to work every day. Mark Dudley, the project manager who oversaw its design and development, summed up the brief neatly: the Tamora was “designed to be got into after a long day at the office.” Think about that. A company famous for cars that demanded skill and occasionally extraordinary patience was building something a tired driver would look forward to, without cutting the engine to 200 horsepower or giving it the suspension of a luxury sedan. Everyday usability didn’t mean removing what made a sports car special. It meant refining it.

And the roof came off. The Tamora kept the open-air experience that had made the Chimaera such a success. It wasn’t built for the grand arrival at a 5-star hotel or a late-night showdown with an Italian supercar. It was built for the unplanned weekend and the detour through the hills, for someone who wanted to drive rather than perform, and I rather like that.

From the factory floor

The playpen. The prototype took shape in a corner of the Blackpool factory known, with good reason, as the playpen.

The window that wouldn’t fit. Fitting glass was always a battle at TVR, and the Tamora’s passenger-side window almost always arrived too big for its opening. Rather than make the suppliers get the size right, the factory changed the body mold to fit the glass.

Beer for the new kids. The new Tamora line took longer per car than the rest of the factory and never got to leave early, so just before Christmas 2003, production engineer Trevor Cooper turned up with cases of beer for them. When everyone else complained, his answer was short: “You get enough perks!”

The catchBut there was still a problem

We can’t discuss the Tamora without discussing reliability. The Speed Six had built a troubled reputation, especially in its early, larger forms, with valve gear and lubrication problems leading to expensive rebuilds. The 3.6 fared better, partly because the lessons were built in from the start and partly because it made its power so high up the rev range that it worked less hard day to day. It still wasn’t immune. This was a hand-built, low-volume car from a company whose ambition often outran its budget, and cooling problems, aging parts and corrosion of the steel chassis could all become serious.

That is where taking on Porsche got complicated. A Boxster came with a consistent ownership experience and an established dealer network. The TVR offered more power, more rarity and far more personality, but also far more uncertainty, and for a car sold as approachable, the lack of ABS and traction control was getting hard to explain by the early 2000s. The Tamora was civilized by TVR standards. It wasn’t necessarily civilized by anyone else’s.

The salesThe cruel mathematics of being overlooked

Dodds counts about 356 Tamoras delivered between 2002 and 2006, an astonishing gap for a car meant to replace the company’s best seller. How could something so capable fail to find buyers?

Part of the answer was its looks. It wasn’t as handsome as the Chimaera, as spectacular as the Tuscan or as purposeful as the Sagaris, and Dodds wonders how many buyers were put off by the styling and how many by the stories about the bigger Speed Six engines. Then there was the price. At £36,500 ($52,600) in 2001, about £78,400 ($103,900) in today’s money, it was up against very capable cars from bigger makers with more reassuring ownership. TVR loyalists had the Tuscan for drama, everyone else had the Boxster, and the Tamora was caught in between.

The cruelest part is that its greatest strength was the hardest thing to sell. Handling balance rarely sells a car from a showroom window; a spectacular shape, a famous badge or an enormous engine does. The Tamora’s gift only showed itself behind the wheel, which may be why the road testers liked it so much more than the buying public did. Dodds counts it among TVR’s most accomplished cars all the same, one that “deserved better recognition.”

The few who did buy one tended to fall hard. Ian Dally’s wife has told him more than once, “you love that car more than me!” He found an early Tuscan too punishing and a Sagaris beyond his budget, and he wouldn’t give up driving without a roof, so after about 6 years with his Chimaera, he bought an unregistered 2005 Tamora in Laser Blue straight off a dealer’s floor. After 9 years and 25,000 miles, it had needed little beyond yearly servicing, a battery, a clutch, a couple of engine mounts and a set of rear tires.

The legacyThe car that quietly shaped what came next

The Tamora’s importance didn’t end with its sales. In 2002, TVR used it as the basis for a coupe, the T350, which grew out of work on a new race car. The T was a nod to the Tamora and the 350 was its horsepower. It made its debut at the NEC in October 2002, with lines McTaggart drew loosely from a 1956 Maserati, the A6G Zagato, which is why early reviewers kept mentioning 1950s Aston Martins.

Its chopped-off tail had a job to do. TVR’s earlier cars all generated some lift at the rear at speed; the Griffith, never tested in a wind tunnel, was estimated to produce about 20 to 30 kg (44 to 66 lb) of it at 120 mph. After hours in the wind tunnel, the T350 came very close to producing downforce instead. And on the T350, TVR built the Sagaris, a car that looked as though it had escaped from a race paddock with no intention of going back. Underneath was an evolution of the supposedly modest Tamora. It may have been a commercial disappointment, but it was never an engineering dead end.

The lessonWhat we missed

The older I get, the more I appreciate cars that don’t try to overwhelm every sense at once. The Cerbera will always hold a special place in my affections, but there is something deeply rewarding about a well-balanced sports car on a good road. A car doesn’t need 600 horsepower or 200 mph to be memorable. Sometimes progress means better steering, a better-judged chassis and a driver with more confidence, and TVR had begun to work out how to make its cars more approachable without making them less interesting. Imagine a properly developed successor with the Tamora’s balance and a more dependable engine. There would have been a place for it, and there still would be. Unfortunately, the company was running out of time. The Tamora stayed in production until the Blackpool factory closed in December 2006, and nothing like it followed.

The characterThe weekend escape artist

Every great TVR seems to have a personality. The Griffith was the hot rod, the Chimaera the gentleman spy on holiday, the Cerbera the family man with a criminal record, the Tuscan the showman and the Sagaris the assassin.

So where does the Tamora fit? I think it is the weekend escape artist, the one who leaves work on Friday afternoon, changes out of his suit, throws a small bag in the trunk and disappears toward the countryside without telling anyone where he’s going. He doesn’t need an audience, and he doesn’t much care what anyone thinks of his looks. He simply knows where the good roads are, and when he finds them, he comes alive.

Every great escape has someone like him. The crowd remembers the showman and the assassin, but nobody remembers the getaway driver, and the good ones make sure of it. Yet this quiet one did more than slip away. The Sagaris was built on what he left behind, so in a sense the assassin learned its trade from him.

The Tamora was not TVR abandoning its rebellious streak. It was TVR discovering that rebellion didn’t always have to be loud, that it could be precise, controlled and genuinely sophisticated. It was never the star of the family. It was the one who quietly got on with the job, performed brilliantly when called upon, and left everyone who really knew him wondering why the others got so much attention. The Tamora proved TVR knew how to make something more than merely fast. It knew how to make something genuinely good. And almost nobody noticed.

If you want one

Service history is everything. evo’s buying guide advises a service every 6,000 miles and setting the valve clearances every 12,000, and in 2013 it suggested budgeting about £1,500 ($2,350) a year, about £2,230 ($2,960) in 2026 money. Early engines wore out their finger followers, since cured with better parts, so look for proof the work has been done.

Then the rest. Check the steel frame carefully, especially around the catalytic converter, test the T5 gearbox for clutch slip and make sure the dampers aren’t leaking.

What they cost. The Classic Valuer puts an average-condition Tamora at about £19,100 ($25,300), and CLASSIC.COM’s market benchmark is $25,267. None was sold new in America, but the first customer cars, from January 2002, turn 25 in January 2027. If you’re in the US, start with The Long Road Home.

Sometimes the greatest sports cars aren’t the ones demanding your attention. They’re the ones that reward you for giving it.
